claims.text: Premelting and melting in Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles are primarily governed by the synergistic effects of high configurational entropy and atomic-size mismatch.
Atomic-size mismatch creates heterogeneous local lattice-strain fields in these nanoparticles.
The heterogeneous strain fields locally lower the melting point.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles should begin developing surface disorder earlier and melt more gradually and inhomogeneously than simpler nanoparticles.
The initial Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles are solid and single phase.
The initial nanoparticles have a uniform chemical distribution.
Atomic-size differences and configurational entropy create local regions with reduced cohesive energy.
Regions of reduced cohesive energy promote stochastic nucleation of premelted zones.
Premelted zones grow and merge as temperature increases, producing spatially distributed rather than sharp melting.
Comparable single-metal or binary nanoparticles generally undergo uniform, abrupt melting without significant surface premelting.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles will have a broader melting-onset and transition-temperature range than size-matched single-metal or binary controls.
Premelting will be observable as partial surface-liquid-layer formation.
Diffuse or broadened XRD peaks will indicate premelting in the HEA nanoparticles.
DSC will show a spread in melting temperatures for the HEA nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism should dominate when compositional complexity and atomic-size disparity are significant.
The mechanism should become less applicable for larger particles or HEAs whose constituent elements have minimal size differences.
Melting onset and premelting-layer extent may depend on synthesis history, particle-size distribution, and measurement sensitivity.
